summary: Defines M3UA, a protocol for carrying SS7 MTP3 user signaling, such as ISUP and SCCP messages, over IP using SCTP. It runs between a Signaling Gateway and a Media Gateway Controller or IP-based signaling endpoint. It was replaced by RFC 4666.

eli5.summary: Telephone companies have a special way of arranging calls. M3UA lets those arrangements ride on internet connections so a computer can take part in the phone network.

questions: how does ss7 mtp3 work over ip
subtitle: Carrying telephone network signaling over the internet.

tldr.problem: Telephone networks use a protocol called SS7 (Signaling System 7) for call setup and management, but these networks need to interwork with IP-based systems like media gateways and softwitches that handle modern voice over IP calls.
tldr.mechanism: M3UA (Message Transfer Part 3-User Adaptation Layer) adapts SS7 signaling messages to travel over IP networks using SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol). It bridges the gap between the telephone signaling network and IP applications by translating between SS7 concepts and IP-based operations.
tldr.outcome: M3UA enabled telephone companies to replace dedicated SS7 links with IP connections, allowing legacy telephone switches to communicate with IP-based call processing systems. RFC 4666 superseded this specification in 2006.

today: RFC 3332 is obsoleted by RFC 4666, which was published in 2006 with updates and clarifications to the M3UA protocol specification.

sections.title: Introduction to M3UA
sections.content:
RFC 3332 defines M3UA (Message Transfer Part 3-User Adaptation Layer), a protocol for transporting SS7 (Signaling System 7) MTP3-User messages such as ISUP (ISDN User Part) and SCCP (Signaling Connection Control Part) over IP networks using SCTP.

M3UA operates between a Signaling Gateway (SG), which terminates traditional SS7 links, and Application Server Processes (ASPs), which are IP-based applications like media gateway controllers. It provides seamless operation of telephone signaling protocols across the boundary between circuit-switched telephone networks and IP networks.
sections.eli5: M3UA is the bridge between two worlds: the old telephone signaling network (SS7) and new IP networks. A signaling gateway sits at the bridge, receives phone signals, and forwards them as internet messages to programs that process calls.

sections.title: Protocol Architecture and Roles
sections.content:
M3UA defines three main types of network elements:

Signaling Gateway Process (SGP): Terminates SS7 MTP2 and MTP3 protocol layers and delivers MTP3-User messages (ISUP, SCCP) over SCTP associations to IP applications. The SGP acts as the interface between the telephone network and the IP domain.

Application Server Process (ASP): An IP-based application instance that receives SS7 messages from a signaling gateway. An ASP might be a media gateway controller or a database server handling telephone transactions.

IP Server Process (IPSP): An IP-based application that uses M3UA in point-to-point mode without a signaling gateway, for direct communication between two IP applications.

M3UA is recommended to use SCTP because of its features like packet-oriented delivery, multi-streaming, and fault tolerance through multi-homing. TCP MAY be used for simpler back-to-back connections without redundancy requirements.
sections.eli5: The signaling gateway (SGP) listens to telephone signals and translates them into messages. Application servers (ASPs) are internet programs that receive these messages. Two IP programs can also talk directly using M3UA without a gateway (IPSP mode).

sections.title: Routing Keys and Message Distribution
sections.content:
M3UA uses Routing Keys and Routing Contexts to direct SS7 messages to the correct application. A Routing Key is a set of SS7 address parameters (such as the destination point code, originating point code, and service indicator) that describes which range of traffic an Application Server should handle. A Routing Context is a unique integer associated with each Routing Key.

When the signaling gateway receives an SS7 message, it compares the message's addressing information against provisioned Routing Keys to determine which Application Server should receive it. The Routing Context in outgoing M3UA messages identifies which logical traffic stream is being carried.

Routing Keys can be provisioned statically through a management interface or dynamically using M3UA's routing key management procedures. This allows flexible configuration where multiple ASPs can handle different ranges of calls or provide redundancy for the same traffic ranges.
sections.eli5: Think of routing keys as address filters. A key says "if a message is going to phone number range 555-1000 to 555-2000, send it to Application Server A." Different application servers handle different phone numbers, just like how different departments in a phone company handle different regions.

sections.title: Message Structure
sections.content:
All M3UA messages begin with an 8-byte Common Message Header containing a version field, a reserved field, a message class, and a message type, followed by a 32-bit message length field. This header is followed by zero or more variable-length parameters in Tag-Length-Value (TLV) format.

Message classes include: Transfer Messages (carrying SS7 payload), SS7 Signaling Network Management (SSNM) Messages (reporting network status like destination unavailable or congestion), ASP State Maintenance (ASPSM) Messages (managing the availability of servers), ASP Traffic Maintenance (ASPTM) Messages (activating or deactivating traffic), and Routing Key Management (RKM) Messages (dynamically provisioning routing).

The message length includes the header and all parameters and any padding bytes. Parameters are padded to 4-byte boundaries for alignment. The protocol carries IP protocol version 1.0.
sections.eli5: An M3UA message has a header that says what kind of message it is (data, status, or control), how long the message is, followed by parameters. Each parameter is labeled with what it contains so the receiver knows how to interpret it.

sections.title: Network Status and Management
sections.content:
M3UA provides mechanisms to report the availability and congestion status of SS7 destinations to remote ASPs, mimicking the behavior of the local MTP3 layer in the traditional telephone network.

When the signaling gateway receives MTP3 management indications (such as MTP-PAUSE when a destination becomes unavailable, or MTP-RESUME when it comes back online), the SGP propagates this status to all connected ASPs using M3UA SSNM messages. This allows IP applications to know immediately if a telephone destination is reachable.

M3UA also supports reporting of congestion, restricted destinations, and user part unavailability. ASPs can indicate their own congestion state to the SG using Signaling Congestion (SCON) messages.
sections.eli5: When a phone line goes down, the signaling gateway tells all the application servers about it using status messages. This way, they do not try to send calls to a number that cannot be reached.

sections.title: Redundancy and Failover
sections.content:
M3UA supports multiple redundancy models. An Application Server can consist of multiple ASPs (Application Server Processes) that share the same Routing Key. The ASPs can be active (currently processing traffic), inactive (standing by), or unavailable (down).

The protocol supports n+k redundancy where n ASPs handle normal traffic and k additional ASPs are available for failover. It also supports 1+1 active/backup and 1+0 simplex (no redundancy) models.

Each ASP maintains state information (active or inactive) that the signaling gateway monitors using ASP State Maintenance Messages (ASPUP, ASPDN, and their acknowledgements). When an active ASP fails, the SG reroutes traffic to another ASP in the same Application Server.
sections.eli5: If a computer handling calls crashes, another computer can take over automatically. Multiple backups can wait in the wings, and the system uses messages to track which ones are ready to go.
